story: On 19 July, Spain beat Argentina 1-0 in extra time at MetLife Stadium to win the World Cup, the country's second. Two months later, Spaniards were back in the streets, this time in anger. The trigger was the televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman named Maricarmen from her Madrid flat, owned by an investment fund; it crystallised years of fury over a housing market in which average rents have nearly doubled in a decade (AFP via Oman Observer).

Protesters pitched a tent city in Madrid's Puerta del Sol. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's minority government proposed two emergency decrees, including a ban on evicting vulnerable tenants until 2030 and limits on purchases by investment funds. On 2 October, the conservative PP, the far-right Vox and the Catalan separatists of Junts, whose votes the government relies on, defeated them. The next day the government said 70,000 people marched in Madrid; organisers claimed half a million. On 5 October, Sánchez called a snap election for 29 November, ten months early, asking voters to choose between joining "the far-right wave" and keeping Spain "a bastion of openness" (Al Jazeera). Polls favour a PP government dependent on Vox. Sánchez is also under fire for corruption cases and for the crisis in Ceuta, where about 70,000 people crossed from Morocco in 48 hours. If he loses, one of Europe's last left-wing governments falls.
briefing.power: A constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system. The prime minister needs the confidence of the 350-seat Congress of Deputies, elected by provincial proportional representation; regional governments, especially in Catalonia and the Basque Country, hold wide powers. King Felipe VI is head of state.
briefing.holders: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez (PSOE), facing an election on 29 November.
